title: Two versions of a correction
topic: 文化与媒体 · 语气、来源与修订责任
paragraphs: The first version of our neighbourhood exhibition described a closed cinema as a place that everyone had loved. It was an attractive sentence, and several visitors recognised their own memories in it. One former employee, however, asked us to change it. She remembered arguments over working hours and people who had stopped going long before the building closed. She was not asking us to remove the affectionate memories. Her objection was to the word everyone: a public description had turned some people’s experience into a claim on behalf of an entire community.

Our small editorial group agreed that the sentence needed attention, but agreement did not settle how to revise it. One person suggested replacing everyone with many people and leaving the rest untouched. Another wanted to remove the sentence altogether. Much as I valued a quick correction, I did not think either option answered the visitor’s concern completely. We needed to show what the original claim had been based on, and to explain why it was being limited. Otherwise, the revised sentence might look more cautious while remaining just as difficult to question.

With the original notes still available, we could separate three interviews from a later summary written by a volunteer. The interviews contained warm accounts of childhood visits; the summary had quietly joined those accounts into a collective voice. Nobody had deliberately invented an interview. The change had happened through ordinary editing: repeated phrases were compressed, differences disappeared, and a convenient subject was supplied. That made the problem more useful to examine, not less serious. If a claim could grow through routine compression, asking editors simply to be honest would not be a sufficient safeguard.

We prepared a new label that attributed the affectionate memories to the people interviewed. A short note explained that other experiences had not been represented in that description. We also kept a record of the earlier wording, with the names of interviewees removed from the public comparison. The purpose was to make the editorial change visible without treating personal details as evidence that every reader was entitled to inspect. Access to a correction did not require unlimited access to the people whose words had contributed to it.

The former employee read the proposed revision. She preferred a shorter explanation and did not want to be presented as the sole person who had challenged the display. Much as we admired the clarity of a story with a named critic and a decisive response, that would have created another misleading simplification. We described the concern without turning her into a representative of every absent voice. Her comments improved our plan, but they did not grant us permission to assign her a public role that she had not chosen.

With the opening date approaching, we narrowed the scope of the review. We checked the labels that made similarly broad claims, rather than pretending to examine the entire archive in a few days. Some labels were revised; others were marked for later investigation. That distinction mattered. A statement that had been reviewed and retained was not the same as one we had not yet checked. We used separate internal marks for those states so that a future editor would not mistake silence for approval.

The corrected display was less smooth than the first version. It contained qualifications, visible sources and an admission that the work was unfinished. Visitors could still enjoy the memories, but they could also see where a claim stopped. We did not regard that as proof that our exhibition had become neutral. Selecting a source and deciding what to leave out remained editorial choices. What changed was the reader’s opportunity to identify those choices and ask a more precise question. A correction had become a way to keep an argument open, rather than a final sentence announcing that the argument was over.
translation: 社区展览的初稿把一家已经关闭的电影院称作“人人喜爱的地方”。这句话动人，几位参观者也在其中认出了自己的记忆。但一位前员工请求修改。她记得对工作时间的争论，也记得有人在建筑关闭很久以前就不再去了。她并非要求删掉温暖记忆，而是反对“人人”：公开说明把一些人的经历变成了替整个社区说话的主张。
小型编辑组同意句子需要处理，但同意并未决定如何修订。一人建议把人人改成许多人，其他不动；另一人想整句删除。尽管我重视快速更正，却认为两种办法都没完全回应关切。我们需要说明原来依据什么，又为何缩小范围。否则新句子可能看似更审慎，却仍然同样难以质疑。
因为原始记录仍在，我们得以区分三份访谈与后来由志愿者写的摘要。访谈有温暖的童年观影记忆；摘要却悄悄把它们拼成了集体声音。没有人故意伪造访谈。变化来自日常编辑：重复被压缩，差异消失，再补上方便的主语。这使问题更值得分析，而非不严重。如果主张能在常规压缩中变大，仅要求编辑诚实并不足以防范。
我们准备了新标签，把温暖记忆明确归于受访者。短注说明另一些经历没有被这段描述呈现。我们还保留旧措辞的记录，同时在公开比较中移去受访者姓名。目的在于使编辑变化可见，而不是把个人细节当成每个读者都有权查看的证据。了解更正不需要无限制了解贡献话语的人。
前员工读了修订稿。她希望说明更短，也不愿被当成唯一挑战展览的人。尽管我们欣赏“具名批评者加果断回应”这种故事的清晰性，它又会制造误导性的简化。我们描述关切，却不把她变成所有缺席声音的代表。她的意见改进计划，但没有授权我们替她安排一个未选择的公开角色。
随着开幕日期临近，我们缩小审阅范围，检查同样作出宽泛主张的标签，而不是假装几天内审完全部档案。有些修改了，另一些标为后续调查。区别很重要：审阅后保留的陈述，与尚未检查的陈述不是一回事。我们用不同内部标记区分，避免未来编辑把沉默误当批准。
更正后的展览不如初稿流畅，有限定、可见来源，也承认工作未完成。访客仍能享受记忆，也能看到主张止于哪里。我们不把这当成展览已经中立的证明；选择来源和省略什么仍是编辑判断。变化在于读者有机会识别这些选择，提出更精确的问题。更正成了保持讨论开放的办法，而非宣布讨论结束的最后一句。

grammar.surface: Much as we admired the clarity
With the original notes still available

questions.prompt: What does the writer see as the main value of the correction?
options: It makes editorial choices traceable and open to more precise questions.
It proves that the exhibition is now completely neutral.
It replaces all personal memories with a single official account.
questions.explanation: The conclusion stresses identifying choices and keeping discussion open, while explicitly rejecting a claim to complete neutrality.

questions.prompt: What did the original notes reveal?
options: A deliberate invention of all three interviews.
A volunteer summary had combined individual memories into a collective claim.
The former employee had requested that no interviews be used.
questions.explanation: Paragraph three distinguishes the interviews from the later summary and describes compression, not wholesale fabrication or a ban on interviews.

questions.prompt: Why distinguish reviewed-and-retained labels from unchecked ones?
options: To ensure every unchanged label can be treated as approved.
To prevent readers from knowing any source exists.
To stop a future editor interpreting lack of change as evidence of review.
questions.explanation: Paragraph six warns that silence can be mistaken for approval; a retained reviewed statement and an unchecked one have different evidential status.

questions.prompt: What does “Much as we admired the clarity …” signal in paragraph five?
options: An appreciation that is acknowledged but does not settle the editorial decision.
A numerical measure of the clarity of every interview.
The sole cause of the decision to name the former employee.
questions.explanation: The following clause rejects the appealing named-critic narrative as another simplification; appreciation is conceded, then qualified.

questions.prompt: Why discuss removing names from the public comparison?
options: To claim that corrections should contain no verifiable wording.
To distinguish transparency about editing from unlimited entitlement to personal information.
To imply that all interviewees demanded the same change.
questions.explanation: Paragraph four makes editorial change visible while limiting access to personal details, preserving a distinction between accountability and personal exposure.

notes: 原创教学情境，不是真实新闻、档案规范或法律建议。
预计用时按每分钟约160个英文单词计算，不是个人速度预测。
